clinical_category: Liver transplant waitlist - anxiety and coping support
blueprint_topic: Therapeutic communication, coping assessment, and support-system resources
stem: A client on the liver-transplant waiting list says, "I can't stop worrying because I have no idea how long I'll wait or whether an organ will come in time." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.A: Acknowledge the uncertainty, assess how the anxiety is affecting coping, give accurate information within the nurse's role, and connect the client with transplant-center or peer-support resources if desired.
options.B: Reassure the client that the wait will probably be short because most liver candidates receive an organ within a predictable period.
options.C: Avoid discussing waitlist concerns because talking about uncertainty usually worsens anxiety and does not help coping.
options.D: Tell the client that waiting time depends only on how long the client has already been listed, so nothing else needs to be discussed.

rationale: A is correct. HRSA/OPTN and SRTR patient resources explain that transplant waiting times vary widely and depend on multiple factors rather than a single predictable timeline. They direct patients to their transplant center for individualized waitlist-status information and identify patient-support resources and support groups as potential sources of help. NCSBN places assessment of coping, support systems, and therapeutic communication within Psychosocial Integrity. B is incorrect because the nurse should not give false reassurance or invent a predictable waiting period. C is nontherapeutic because avoiding the client's expressed concern does not support coping. D is incorrect because waiting time is influenced by multiple factors, including medical urgency and donor/matching factors, not simply time already accrued. The final item focuses on therapeutic support and accurate uncertainty rather than implying that peer support is mandatory or that the nurse can predict an individual transplant date.
educational_objective: Support transplant-waitlist anxiety by acknowledging uncertainty, assessing coping, providing accurate role-appropriate information, and connecting clients with individualized transplant-center or peer-support resources without giving false reassurance about timing.
source_organization: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN); Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR)
source_document_title: Transplant Process; Patient Information Letter; Getting Listed; Getting a Transplant
source_version_date: HRSA/OPTN patient resources last reviewed 2025-12; current SRTR patient resources accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: HRSA/OPTN 'Transplant Process' → 'Waiting times': waiting times vary widely and depend on multiple patient/donor factors; 'Patient notification': clients should discuss individual waitlist status with the transplant team. HRSA/OPTN 'Patient Information Letter' → OPTN patient services provides general waitlist information but directs individual medical/status questions to the transplant hospital. SRTR 'Getting Listed' → wait time varies from days/weeks to years and centers may connect patients with local support groups. SRTR 'Getting a Transplant' → waiting-list section: periodic follow-up, staying healthy, family/friend involvement, stress/coping and support resources.
source_claim_supported: Current HRSA/OPTN and SRTR resources directly support the uncertainty and multifactorial nature of transplant waiting time, referral back to the transplant center for individualized status information, and availability of support resources/groups during the transplant journey.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 14): assess psychosocial factors influencing care; assess client support system; assess ability to cope with life changes and provide support; use therapeutic communication techniques.
correction_summary: Retained the valid waitlist-anxiety construct but replaced the vague UNOS/AASLD citation with current HRSA/OPTN and SRTR patient resources. Rewrote the item as a therapeutic response that acknowledges uncertainty, avoids false reassurance, and uses individualized support resources rather than implying a predictable transplant timeline.
audit_findings: The source answer was directionally appropriate but used a vague combined UNOS/AASLD source without a precise locator.
Fresh HRSA/OPTN and SRTR review confirms transplant wait times are uncertain and multifactorial and that individual status questions belong with the transplant center.
SRTR also supports use of patient support resources and local support groups as optional aids during the transplant journey.
Distractors test false reassurance, avoidance of expressed anxiety, and waiting-time-only misinformation; none is therapeutically defensible.

Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct therapeutic response with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, invented waiting-time estimate, locator defect, blueprint mismatch, or unresolved conflict.
